html:
"Proto-Thai cultures" is the map's label, in 400 BCE, for the early Tai-speaking peoples of what is now southern China, mainly Guangxi and its neighbours. Their languages belong to the Kra-Dai family, which includes Thai, Lao, Shan and Zhuang.

Chinese writers lumped the southern peoples together as the Hundred Yue. Many grew rice in wet fields, kept water buffalo, built houses on stilts and traveled by river. Bronze drums of the Đông Sơn type were shared across much of this southern world. Qin armies pushed into the region after 221 BCE, and the kingdom of Nanyue ruled much of it until the Han conquest of 111 BCE.

Linguists think Tai speakers moved slowly southwest from this region during the first millennium CE and after, down the river valleys into what are now Laos, Thailand, Myanmar's Shan State and northeast India. By the 1200s Tai rulers had founded kingdoms such as Lan Na and Sukhothai, part of the chart's Sukhothai and Ayutthaya bar. The Zhuang, who stayed behind, are today the largest minority in China.
